lessons.title: Divide Whole Numbers by Fractions
lessons.objective: I can explain what dividing a whole number by a fraction means — how many pieces fit, or how much is in one whole — find the quotient with a model or by multiplying by the reciprocal, and check it by multiplying.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain why multiplying by the reciprocal works, using the words fraction, reciprocal, quotient, and Keep, Change, Flip.

concept.heading: How do I divide a whole number by a fraction?
concept.intro: Dividing a whole number by a fraction asks how many of those pieces fit, or how much is in one whole. 4 ÷ 1/2 counts halves: every whole holds 2 halves, so the answer is 4 × 2 = 8. That is why the shortcut called Keep, Change, Flip works — dividing by a fraction gives the same answer as multiplying by its reciprocal. Check by multiplying: 8 × 1/2 = 4.
concept.keyIdea: Dividing Whole Numbers by Fractions. Formula: a ÷ (b/c) = a × (c/b). 1. Name the question: 4 ÷ 1/2 asks how many 1/2s fit in 4. 2. Count with a model: each whole holds 2 halves, so 4 wholes hold 4 × 2 = 8 halves. 3. Shortcut: multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor, 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6 × 4/3 = 8, then check by multiplying: 8 × 3/4 = 6

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Agent Park has 4 pounds of powder and each bag holds 1/2 pound. I want 4 ÷ 1/2.
Each pound fills 2 half-pound bags, so 4 pounds fill 4 × 2 = 8 bags.
That is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal of 1/2: 4 × 2/1 = 8. Dividing by 1/2 doubles the count, because every whole holds 2 halves.
Check by multiplying: 8 bags × 1/2 pound = 4 pounds. So 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8. He can fill 8 bags.
linesEs: El agente Park tiene 4 libras de polvo y cada bolsa guarda 1/2 libra. Quiero 4 ÷ 1/2.
Cada libra llena 2 bolsas de media libra, así que 4 libras llenan 4 × 2 = 8 bolsas.
Eso es lo mismo que multiplicar por el recíproco de 1/2: 4 × 2/1 = 8. Dividir entre 1/2 duplica la cuenta, porque cada entero tiene 2 medios.
Compruebo multiplicando: 8 bolsas × 1/2 libra = 4 libras. Entonces 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8. Puede llenar 8 bolsas.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's try 3 ÷ 1/4 together. How many 1/4s fit in 3? Each whole holds 4 fourths.
So 3 wholes hold 3 × 4 = 12 fourths — the same as 3 × 4/1, multiplying by the reciprocal.
linesEs: Probemos 3 ÷ 1/4 juntos. ¿Cuántos 1/4 caben en 3? Cada entero tiene 4 cuartos.
Así que 3 enteros tienen 3 × 4 = 12 cuartos, lo mismo que 3 × 4/1, multiplicar por el recíproco.

vocabulary.definition: Find how many fractional groups fit in a whole number by multiplying by the reciprocal.
A counting number with no fraction or decimal, like 0, 1, 2, 3.
vocabulary.example: 4 is a whole number; as a fraction it is 4/1

vocabulary.definition: A number that shows part of a whole, like 3/4.
vocabulary.example: 1/2 means 1 out of 2 equal parts — like cutting a sandwich in half and taking one piece

vocabulary.definition: A fraction turned upside down.
vocabulary.example: The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. Flip the fraction to divide: 6 ÷ 2/3 = 6 × 3/2

vocabulary.definition: A shortcut for dividing fractions: keep the first number, change ÷ to ×, flip the second. It works because dividing by a fraction gives the same answer as multiplying by its reciprocal.
The answer when you divide.

lessons.title: Divide Mixed Numbers
lessons.objective: I can explain what dividing with mixed numbers means, rewrite them as improper fractions, find the quotient with common denominators or by multiplying by the reciprocal, and check it by multiplying.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my steps and why they work, using the words mixed number, improper fraction, convert, reciprocal, and simplify.

concept.heading: How do I divide with mixed numbers?
concept.intro: A mixed number, like 3 1/2, has a whole part and a fraction part. Before you can divide, you change each mixed number into an improper fraction (top heavier than bottom). Then ask how many of the divisor fit — with common denominators or by multiplying by the reciprocal — and check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.
concept.keyIdea: Dividing Mixed Numbers. 1. Convert each mixed number to an improper fraction: 3 1/2 = 7/2. 2. Name the question and divide: 7/2 ÷ 1/4 asks how many 1/4s fit in 7/2. With common denominators, 7/2 = 14/4, and 14 fourths ÷ 1 fourth = 14, or multiply by the reciprocal: 7/2 × 4/1 = 28/2 = 14. 3. Simplify, then check by multiplying: 14 × 1/4 = 14/4 = 3 1/2

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Agent Chen has a 3 1/2-mile route cut into 1/4-mile segments. I want 3 1/2 ÷ 1/4.
First I convert 3 1/2. Multiply the whole by the bottom: 3 × 2 = 6. Add the top: 6 + 1 = 7. So 3 1/2 = 7/2.
Now I ask how many 1/4s fit in 7/2. In fourths, 7/2 = 14/4, and 14 fourths ÷ 1 fourth = 14 — the common-denominator method.
The reciprocal shortcut gives the same answer: 7/2 × 4/1 = 28/2 = 14.
linesEs: La agente Chen tiene una ruta de 3 1/2 millas dividida en tramos de 1/4 de milla. Quiero 3 1/2 ÷ 1/4.
Primero convierto 3 1/2. Multiplico el entero por el denominador: 3 × 2 = 6. Sumo el numerador: 6 + 1 = 7. Entonces 3 1/2 = 7/2.
Ahora pregunto cuántos 1/4 caben en 7/2. En cuartos, 7/2 = 14/4, y 14 cuartos ÷ 1 cuarto = 14: el método de denominadores comunes.
El atajo del recíproco da la misma respuesta: 7/2 × 4/1 = 28/2 = 14.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's try 2 1/2 ÷ 1/2. First convert 2 1/2: 2 × 2 = 4, plus 1 = 5, so 2 1/2 = 5/2.
How many halves fit in 5/2? Five — the halves are already counted: 5/2 ÷ 1/2 = 5. The reciprocal shortcut agrees: 5/2 × 2/1 = 10/2 = 5.
linesEs: Probemos 2 1/2 ÷ 1/2. Primero convierte 2 1/2: 2 × 2 = 4, más 1 = 5, así que 2 1/2 = 5/2.
¿Cuántos medios caben en 5/2? Cinco: los medios ya están contados: 5/2 ÷ 1/2 = 5. El atajo del recíproco coincide: 5/2 × 2/1 = 10/2 = 5.

vocabulary.definition: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions, then multiply by the reciprocal.
A whole number plus a fraction, like 2 1/3.
vocabulary.example: 2 1/3 means 2 wholes and 1/3 more — picture 2 full circles and 1/3 of another

vocabulary.definition: A fraction where the top is bigger than or equal to the bottom, like 7/4.
vocabulary.example: 7/3 is improper because 7 > 3. It equals 2 1/3 as a mixed number.

vocabulary.definition: To change a number to a new form but keep the same value.
vocabulary.example: 2 1/3 → multiply 2 × 3 = 6, add 1 → 7/3. Same value, different form.

vocabulary.definition: To write a fraction with smaller numbers that names the same amount, like 2/4 = 1/2.
A fraction turned upside down. Dividing by a fraction gives the same answer as multiplying by its reciprocal.
vocabulary.example: The reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3. To divide by 3/4, multiply by 4/3.

investigate: How many 3/4-unit pieces fit into 5 1/2 units? Predict before checking.
Separate the exact quotient from the number of complete pieces.
Check the used length and remaining ribbon with multiplication and subtraction.
create: Write a ribbon order with a mixed-number length and fractional piece size. Report the exact quotient, whole pieces, and remaining length with units.

feedback: 2 is 6 ÷ 3 — that divides by 3 instead of by 1/3. Each whole holds 3 thirds: 6 × 3 = 18.
3 is smaller than 6, but dividing by 1/3 counts thirds, so the answer is bigger than 6: 6 × 3 = 18.
6/3 is 6 × 1/3 — that finds a third of 6. Count thirds instead: 6 × 3 = 18.
hints: 6 ÷ 1/3 asks how many 1/3-size pieces fit into 6 wholes. Predict: bigger or smaller than 6?
Use the reciprocal shortcut: keep the 6, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor 1/3.
The flip turns 1/3 into 3/1. Set up 6 × 3 and finish the multiplication.

feedback: 3/5 is 3 × 1/5 — that finds a fifth of 3. Count fifths instead: each whole holds 5, so 3 × 5 = 15.
5/3 flips the wrong number. Only the divisor 1/5 flips, to 5: 3 × 5 = 15.
8 is 3 + 5. Each whole holds 5 fifths, so multiply: 3 × 5 = 15.
hints: The total is 3 wholes and each piece is 1/5 — every whole holds several fifths.
Multiply by the reciprocal: keep 3, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/5 upside down.
1/5 flips to 5/1. Multiply 3 by 5 to count all the fifths.

support.explanation: 10 ÷ 1/4 = 10 × 4/1 = 40. There are 40 quarter-size pieces in 10 wholes.
feedback: 2.5 is 10 ÷ 4 — that divides by 4 instead of by 1/4. Each whole holds 4 fourths: 10 × 4 = 40.
10/4 is 10 × 1/4 — that finds a fourth of 10. Count fourths instead: 10 × 4 = 40.
14 is 10 + 4. Each whole holds 4 fourths, so multiply: 10 × 4 = 40.
hints: You're counting 1/4-size pieces inside 10 wholes — every whole holds more than one.
Keep 10, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor 1/4 before multiplying.
1/4 becomes 4/1, so the problem turns into 10 × 4. Work that product out.

feedback: 2.5 is 5 ÷ 2 — that divides by 2 instead of by 1/2. Each whole holds 2 halves: 5 × 2 = 10.
5/2 is 5 × 1/2 — that finds half of 5. Count halves instead: 5 × 2 = 10.
7 is 5 + 2. Each whole holds 2 halves, so multiply: 5 × 2 = 10.
hints: How many 1/2-size pieces fit into 5 wholes? Each whole holds more than one half.
Multiply by the reciprocal: keep 5, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/2.
1/2 flips to 2/1 — multiply 5 × 2 and check your product against the choices.

steps: Multiply by the reciprocal: Kept the 4 and changed ÷ to ×, but forgot to flip: 4 × 1/5
support.explanation: Flip the divisor 1/5 to its reciprocal 5/1 before multiplying: 4 × 5/1 = 20. The mistake was multiplying by 1/5 instead of flipping it to 5. (The answer should be larger than 4, not smaller.)
hints: After 'Change,' you still have to 'Flip' the second fraction.
1/5 flips to 5/1, so 4 × 5 = 20 — dividing by a fraction less than 1 makes the answer bigger.

feedback: 1 1/8 is 3/2 × 3/4 — that multiplies without flipping. 3/2 = 6/4, and 6 fourths ÷ 3 fourths = 2.
3/4 is the divisor, not the quotient. 1 1/2 = 6/4, and 6 fourths hold 2 groups of 3 fourths.
9/8 is 3/2 × 3/4 — the divisor was never flipped. Multiply by the reciprocal: 3/2 × 4/3 = 12/6 = 2.
hints: 1 1/2 is a mixed number — it has to become one improper fraction before you divide.
Convert: whole × denominator + numerator (1 × 2 + 1), then multiply by the reciprocal with 3/4.
1 1/2 = 3/2. Flip 3/4 to 4/3 and set up 3/2 × 4/3 — multiply across, then simplify.

feedback: 6/5 multiplies 3 × 2 and keeps the 5. Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.
15/5 is just the 3 wholes. Add the 2 fifths too: 15/5 + 2/5 = 17/5.
32/5 writes the 3 and the 2 side by side. Use 3 × 5 + 2 = 17: 17/5.
hints: Converting keeps the denominator 5 the same — only the top number changes.
New numerator = whole × denominator + old numerator.
Compute 3 × 5 first, then add the 2. Put that sum over 5 and find the match.

feedback: Check 1 1/2 by multiplying: 1 1/2 × 3/4 = 9/8, not 2 1/4. 2 1/4 = 9/4, and 9 fourths ÷ 3 fourths = 3.
2 1/3 keeps the 2 and divides only the fraction part (1/4 ÷ 3/4 = 1/3). Convert first: 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 3.
9/16 is less than 1, but 3/4 fits into 2 1/4 more than once. 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 9 ÷ 3 = 3.
hints: Convert 2 1/4 to an improper fraction before anything else.
2 × 4 + 1 gives the new numerator over 4. Then flip the divisor 3/4 to 4/3.
Set up your improper fraction × 4/3 — the fours cancel, leaving an easy division.

feedback: 3 1/8 keeps the 3 and works only on the 1/2. Convert first: 3 1/2 = 7/2, then 7/2 × 4 = 28/2 = 14.
7/8 is 7/2 × 1/4 — the divisor was never flipped. Each whole holds 4 fourths: 7/2 × 4 = 14.
Check 13/4 by multiplying: 13/4 × 1/4 = 13/16, not 3 1/2. Rename 3 1/2 in fourths and count them.
hints: Two steps: convert 3 1/2 first, then divide by 1/4.
3 × 2 + 1 gives the improper fraction over 2. Then flip 1/4 to 4/1.
Set up 7/2 × 4/1 — multiply across and simplify. The answer should be much bigger than 3.

support.explanation: The student forgot to flip the divisor. Multiplying by the reciprocal means 3/4 becomes 4/3. So 3/2 ÷ 3/4 = 3/2 × 4/3 = 12/6 = 2, not 1 1/8.
hints: Look at the reciprocal step — did the divisor get flipped?
To divide by 3/4, multiply by its reciprocal 4/3: 3/2 × 4/3 = 2.

feedback: 2/18 is 2/3 ÷ 6 — the dividend and divisor are switched. Ask how many 2/3s fit in 6.
4 is 6 × 2/3 — the divisor was never flipped. 6 ÷ 2/3 = 6 × 3/2 = 18/2 = 9.
12 is 6 × 2 — it multiplies by the numerator. Multiply by the reciprocal 3/2: 6 × 3/2 = 9.
hints: The divisor is 2/3 — not a unit fraction — so the flip matters even more here.
Keep 6, change ÷ to ×, and flip the whole fraction 2/3 (both numbers trade places).
2/3 flips to 3/2, giving 6 × 3/2. Multiply, then simplify the result before choosing.

core.prompt: Agent Park's 6 pounds of evidence powder fill 3/4 of a storage tub. How many pounds fill a WHOLE tub? (6 ÷ 3/4 asks how much is in one whole tub.)
core.explanation: 3 fourths of the tub hold 6 pounds, so 1 fourth holds 6 ÷ 3 = 2 pounds and the whole tub (4 fourths) holds 4 × 2 = 8 pounds. The shortcut agrees: 6 × 4/3 = 24/3 = 8. Check: 3/4 × 8 = 6.
feedback: 4 1/2 is 6 × 3/4 — that finds 3/4 OF the 6 pounds. The 6 pounds is already 3/4 of the tub, so a whole tub holds more.
2 pounds is only 1/4 of the tub (6 ÷ 3). A whole tub is 4 of those fourths.
6 3/4 adds 6 and 3/4. Find what 1/4 of the tub holds, then build all 4 fourths.
hints: The 6 pounds fill only part of the tub. Which part?
If 3 fourths hold 6 pounds, what does 1 fourth hold?
Multiply by 4 for the whole tub, then check: 3/4 × your answer = 6.

core.prompt: A 5-foot strip of evidence tape is 1/3 of a full roll. How long is the full roll? (5 ÷ 1/3 asks how much is in one whole roll.)
core.explanation: 5 feet is one third of the roll, and a whole roll is 3 thirds: 5 ÷ 1/3 = 5 × 3 = 15 feet. Check by multiplying: 1/3 × 15 = 5.
feedback: 5/3 is 5 × 1/3 — that finds a third of the strip. The 5 feet is already one third of the roll, so the roll is longer.
8 is 5 + 3. A whole roll is 3 groups of 5 feet, so multiply: 5 × 3 = 15.
1/15 divides in the wrong order (1/3 ÷ 5). The known length, 5 feet, is what gets divided by 1/3.
hints: The 5 feet is only one third of the roll.
How many thirds make a whole roll?
5 ÷ 1/3 = 5 × 3. Check: 1/3 × your answer = 5.

steps: Multiply by the reciprocal: Flipped the wrong number — wrote 1/8 × 3/4 instead of 8 × 4/3
core.explanation: Keep the dividend 8 the same and flip only the divisor: 8 × 4/3 = 32/3 = 10 2/3. The mistake was flipping the whole number 8 into 1/8 instead of flipping the divisor 3/4 into 4/3.
hints: Only the divisor (the fraction you are dividing by) gets flipped — the 8 stays as 8.

core.prompt: A baker has 2 1/4 cups of butter. Each batch of cookies needs 3/4 cup of butter. How many batches can the baker make?
feedback: Check 1 1/2 by multiplying: 1 1/2 × 3/4 = 9/8 cups, not 2 1/4 cups. 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 3 batches.
2 batches use only 2 × 3/4 = 1 1/2 cups — 3/4 cup is left, enough for one more batch: 3.
6 batches would need 6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2 cups — twice the butter the baker has.
hints: The butter total, 2 1/4 cups, is the dividend; each batch's 3/4 cup is the divisor.
Convert 2 1/4 to fourths, then ask how many groups of three fourths fit.
2 1/4 = 9/4. Bundle those nine fourths into groups of 3 and count the batches you form.

core.prompt: Agent Chen has walked 2 1/4 miles, which is 3/4 of her whole route. How long is the whole route? (2 1/4 ÷ 3/4 asks how much is in one whole route.)
core.explanation: 2 1/4 = 9/4. Three fourths of the route is 9/4 miles, so one fourth is 9/4 ÷ 3 = 3/4 mile and the whole route (4 fourths) is 4 × 3/4 = 3 miles. Shortcut: 9/4 × 4/3 = 36/12 = 3. Check: 3/4 × 3 = 9/4 = 2 1/4.
feedback: 1 11/16 is 9/4 × 3/4 — that finds 3/4 OF the distance walked. The 2 1/4 miles is already 3/4 of the route, so the route is longer.
1/3 divides in the wrong order (3/4 ÷ 9/4). The distance walked, 2 1/4 miles, is what gets divided by 3/4.
2 1/3 keeps the 2 and divides only the fraction part. Convert first: 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 3.
hints: The 2 1/4 miles is only part of the route. Which part?
Convert 2 1/4 to fourths: 9/4. If 3 fourths of the route is 9/4 miles, what is 1 fourth?
Multiply by 4 for the whole route, then check: 3/4 × your answer = 2 1/4.

core.prompt: A 4 1/2-cup jar of fingerprint gel fills exactly 1 1/2 test kits. How much gel is in ONE kit? (4 1/2 ÷ 1 1/2 asks how much is in one whole kit.)
core.explanation: 4 1/2 = 9/2 and 1 1/2 = 3/2. One and a half kits hold 9/2 cups, so half a kit holds 9/2 ÷ 3 = 3/2 cups and a whole kit holds 2 × 3/2 = 3 cups. Shortcut: 9/2 × 2/3 = 18/6 = 3. Check: 1 1/2 × 3 = 4 1/2.
feedback: 6 3/4 is 9/2 × 3/2 — that multiplies. The jar fills more than one kit, so one kit holds less than the jar.
1/3 divides in the wrong order (3/2 ÷ 9/2). The gel in the jar, 4 1/2 cups, is what gets divided.
4 1/3 keeps the 4 and divides only the fraction parts. Convert first: 9/2 ÷ 3/2 = 3.
hints: The jar fills MORE than one kit, so one kit holds less than 4 1/2 cups.
Convert both: 4 1/2 = 9/2 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.
9/2 ÷ 3/2 = 9 halves ÷ 3 halves. Check: 1 1/2 × your answer = 4 1/2.

core.explanation: The student divided before converting the mixed number. First convert: 3 1/3 = 10/3. Then 10/3 ÷ 2/3 = 10/3 × 3/2 = 30/6 = 5, not 3 1/2.
hints: Did the student convert 3 1/3 to an improper fraction before dividing?
Convert 3 1/3 to 10/3 first, then 10/3 × 3/2 = 5.

stretch.prompt: A pizza shop has 8 whole pizzas. Each serving is 2/3 of a pizza. How many servings can they make? Write and solve an equation, then explain why the answer is greater than 8.
stretch.frame: The equation is 8 ÷ 2/3 = ___. Using the reciprocal shortcut: 8 × 3/2 = ___. The answer is greater than 8 because ___.
stretch.explanation: The question asks how many 2/3-pizza servings fit in 8 pizzas, so the equation is 8 ÷ 2/3. Multiplying by the reciprocal gives 8 × 3/2 = 24/2 = 12 servings. The count beats 8 because each serving is smaller than a whole pizza, so every pizza makes more than one serving.
hints: Re-read: 8 whole pizzas, and each serving takes 2/3 of one pizza — servings are smaller than a pizza.

stretch.prompt: A detective has a rope that is 5 1/4 feet long. She needs to cut it into pieces that are each 3/4 foot for tying evidence tags. How many pieces can she cut? Write the equation, show each step (convert, the reciprocal shortcut, multiply, simplify), and verify your answer.
